description:
Start with a real project

Trim the clip around a clear opening and one useful point. Create a separate crop for each important placement.

Review the first version

Read captions on a phone before export. Break lines at natural pauses and move the captions if they cover a face or a demonstration.

Check the final result

Before a broadcast, rehearse with the real microphone and camera. Check the connection, audio levels and what happens when a guest drops out.

Frequently asked questions

Can a livestream become a short clip?

Choose one exchange that makes sense on its own, then trim around it and add a short caption for context.

Browse related tools on SEOGBTools.

Plan the short clip and live show together

Wave.video brings video editing and live streaming into one browser tool. A small team can use the editor to prepare a short social clip and use the streaming studio for a longer demonstration. Start with the audience's question. A shop that sells lights might want to show how to place a desk lamp beside a monitor. The live show can demonstrate several setups, while the short clip answers one question about glare.

Make a simple run sheet with an opening, the main demonstration, and time for questions. Add the camera view and the person responsible for each part. If two people are hosting, decide who will watch comments while the other shows the product. Agree on a cue for moving between scenes so the presenter knows when to pause.

Edit a social clip from one useful moment

Choose a section that makes sense by itself. If the presenter says “here is the second option,” start a few seconds earlier or add a caption that explains what they are comparing. Give viewers the result early. A clip about glare can show the bright reflection first, then move the lamp and show what changed.

Trim the clip before adding titles and music. Watch the edited sequence with sound off. Add a short opening line or caption if the action needs context. Keep the text away from the bottom edge where social apps may place buttons or descriptions. When the same clip goes on a website, use a wider crop if it gives the viewer a better view of the full desk.

Check captions and run a private rehearsal

Read the captions while the video plays at normal speed. Break long lines where someone would naturally pause. Check product names, measurements, and any words that sound alike. If the captions cover a demonstration, move them or use a different crop. A viewer should be able to see the result and read the explanation at the same time.

Before going live, rehearse with the actual microphone, camera, and internet connection. Have someone watch a test from a separate device and report what they hear. Ask them to check whether the presenter and any shared video play at similar levels. Keep a simple backup plan for a guest who cannot join, such as moving to a second example or taking a few prepared questions.

What to confirm about group buy access

Check whether the SEOGBTools offer supports the editor, export settings, and streaming workflow you plan to use. Ask about any limits that could affect your event, such as the streaming destinations, guest seats, or recording access. Save a local copy of approved videos, captions, and show notes where your team can find them later.

For a project built mainly from still photos, see the Animoto product guide. For a static event card or thumbnail, see Stencil.

Decide what the audience should see first

Picture a small kitchen shop preparing a live demonstration of three ways to use a compact blender. The team has a host, one camera, and thirty minutes. If the audience mostly wants to know whether the blender fits under a shelf, the most useful opening is a view of the counter with the blender in place. The host can give the height, then show how much extra room the lid needs. The other demonstrations can follow once the first question has an answer.

Write the first thirty seconds before planning any graphics. Include the subject, what viewers will see, and why it matters. Avoid spending the opening listing every detail about the company. Someone who joined from a social post should recognize the topic right away. Give a short reminder of the topic between sections so people arriving late can catch up.

Give each camera view a job. A wide shot can show where everything sits. A close view can show the switch, the lid, or the amount of space beside the blender. If you only have one camera, plan when you will move it. A host can pause between steps, move the camera, and tell the audience what detail they are about to see. Try the movement once with the microphone on to catch handling noise.

Build a library of clips you can reuse

Make a folder for the source clips, still images, audio, and approved exports. Give the source files names that describe the action. A file called blender-lid-closeup is easier to find later than one called clip-seven. Keep the camera originals separate from edited files so you can make another crop without losing the first version.

Before uploading material to a browser editor, check that you have permission to use it. A product photo supplied by a manufacturer may have conditions attached. A guest may have agreed to appear in a live session without agreeing to appear in an advertisement made from that session. Confirm how the material will be used while everyone still remembers the plan.

If a project depends on stock material, record where it came from and what use the license covers. This helps when a client asks for proof later or you want to reuse a clip in a paid campaign. Check the terms for the specific asset and the account through which it was obtained. Keep the original note with the project so the next editor can find it.

Make separate cuts for separate jobs

Start with one main version. Then list the changes needed for each destination. A website version might spend more time showing dimensions. A short social cut may need to show the result in the opening frame. A clip for a customer email might focus on one common question and point readers to the full guide.

When you change the frame, play the complete edit again. A wide shot can lose both the host and the product when cropped vertically. You can switch to a detail shot for that moment or use a layout that gives the image room. If a short line of text splits in an awkward place, rewrite it for the narrow frame and check the result on a phone.

Use the last few seconds to make the next step clear. A social clip might ask viewers to watch the full replay. A product page clip could point to a comparison table beside the video. Keep the important link or instruction in the page or caption as well. A viewer may pause the clip or watch it with a setting that changes how much of the frame they can see.

Prepare a livestream guests can join easily

Send guests a short note with the start time, the time zone, and when they should arrive for a check. Give them the topic and the first question so they can prepare a short opening. Ask them to use the device, camera, and microphone they will use during the show. A test on one device gives you little information about a different setup.

Have each person speak at normal volume in the rehearsal. Listen for room echo, background music, and sound from other devices. Ask the guest to turn off any notifications that could appear during screen sharing. Prepare a clean browser window for demonstrations and check what is visible before sharing it.

Keep the show plan somewhere the host can see without turning away from the camera. Include rough time marks, the order of guests, and a note for questions. Leave time to change between demonstrations. If a segment runs long, the host should know which example can be dropped without losing the main point.

Plan for a connection problem

Decide who will act if a camera or microphone stops working. A co-host can keep talking while the presenter checks their setup. If the show has one host, prepare an example or a still image that can hold the viewer's attention while the issue is fixed. Practice moving to that example so the switch feels natural.

Write down the order for recovering from a common problem. If a guest loses audio, give them a clear signal, continue with a question or demonstration, and bring them back once they can be heard. If a shared clip plays without sound, explain the part that matters and give viewers a link later if the clip is available to share.

After the rehearsal, write one line about each issue and who owns the fix. A note such as “guest microphone sounded quiet during the demo” is easier to act on than “audio needs work.” Run a brief follow-up check if the person changes equipment or moves to a different room.

Publish a replay that people can use

Watch enough of the recording to check the opening, the main demonstration, and the ending. If the first minutes are setup time, see whether you can trim the replay or add a clear time marker in its description. Give viewers a short explanation of what they can learn before they press play.

Keep the original recording in an approved folder. Save the public version and any short clips with clear names. If the replay includes a temporary offer, decide whether the offer can stay in the video after it ends. Put current terms next to the replay so viewers know where to check them.

A good replay description gives the subject, the date if it matters, and a short list of sections. For a product demonstration, you can name the tools shown and the question each part answers. If you publish a caption track, compare it with the final recording. Trimming the opening can change the timing of captions made from an earlier cut.

Review what happened after release

Pick one result that matches the job of each video. For a live class, look at the questions viewers asked and whether they understood the demonstration. For a short clip, see whether people reached the point where you show the answer. For a product page video, check whether customers still ask about the detail it was made to explain.

Save those observations beside the project. If viewers ask where to find the dimensions, add that information earlier or make the page link easier to see. If the same guest setup causes problems twice, change the rehearsal checklist. Keep a record of the change so you can see whether it helps on the next show.

More questions about Wave.video

What should I test before using it for a client event?

Use a short rehearsal with the same guest count and devices you expect to use. Check the account's available destinations and whether you can get the recording in the format the client needs. Ask someone to watch from the intended destination and confirm that they can hear both the host and guest.

Can the same captions work for every cut?

Check each cut separately. If you change the start time, remove a section, or move a demonstration, captions from the first version may play at the wrong time. The location of the captions can also need a change when you move from a wide to a tall frame.

How much should I prepare for a first broadcast?

Prepare one clear subject, a short opening, and a backup example. Rehearse the steps that involve switching views or playing a clip. Give the host room to answer questions naturally, especially when an audience member asks for a detail that is already part of the demonstration.

Which features should I ask about before ordering?

Start with the feature that would stop your work if it were unavailable. For one team that may be an export setting. For another it may be the ability to bring in a guest or stream to a certain account. Confirm the current terms for the offer you plan to use.
